sections.title: Quantization of Energy
objectives: Explain Max Planck’s contribution to the development of quantum mechanics.
Explain why atomic spectra indicate quantization.

misconceptions.claim: An electron is a small ball that orbits the nucleus.
misconceptions.correction: It has no orbit. It occupies a quantum state, and the orbit picture is only a picture.

misconceptions.claim: The energy of a photon is proportional to its wavelength.
misconceptions.correction: It is proportional to its frequency, $E = hf$, so a longer wavelength means a lower energy. This is why the blue end of the spectrum carries more energy per photon than the red end.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-3, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the wavelength reading as an option.

summary: The first indication that energy is sometimes quantized came from blackbody radiation, which is the emission of EM radiation by an object with an emissivity of 1.
Planck recognized that the energy levels of the emitting atoms and molecules were quantized, with only the allowed values of E=n+12hf, where n is any non-negative integer (0, 1, 2, 3, …).
h is Planck’s constant, whose value is h=6.626× 10-34 J ⋅ s.

authored_exercises.stem: What did Planck propose about the energy of oscillators in a black body?
authored_exercises.answer: That their energy is quantized in whole-number multiples of hf.
solution: Classical physics allowed any energy for an oscillator.
Planck found he had to restrict the energy to E = nhf.
This quantization explained the observed black-body spectrum.

authored_exercises.stem: A photon has energy 2.0 eV. Express this energy in joules. Take 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
solution: Multiply the energy in electronvolts by the conversion factor.

sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source section on Quantization of Energy has no worked example; the teaching text derives the key results and the practice set applies them.

sections.title: The Photoelectric Effect
objectives: Determine the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons ejected by photons of one energy or wavelength, when given the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons for a different photon energy or wavelength.

misconceptions.claim: The kinetic energy of the electrons emitted in the photoelectric effect is set by the intensity of the light.
misconceptions.correction: It is set by the frequency, $K = hf - \phi$. The intensity decides how many electrons come out, not how fast they are, which is the observation that told Bohr the light was quantised.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-4, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the intensity reading as an option.

summary: The photoelectric effect is the process in which EM radiation ejects electrons from a material.
Einstein proposed photons to be quanta of EM radiation having energy E=hf, where f is the frequency of the radiation.
All EM radiation is composed of photons. As Einstein explained, all characteristics of the photoelectric effect are due to the interaction of individual photons with individual electrons.

sections.title: Photon Energies and the Electromagnetic Spectrum
objectives: Explain the relationship between the energy of a photon in joules or electron volts and its wavelength or frequency.
Calculate the number of photons per second emitted by a monochromatic source of specific wavelength and power.

misconceptions.claim: A brighter light of the same colour produces photons of higher energy.
misconceptions.correction: The energy of a photon depends on its frequency, E = hf. A brighter light of the same colour contains more photons per second, not more energetic ones.

summary: Photon energy is responsible for many characteristics of EM radiation, being particularly noticeable at high frequencies.
Photons have both wave and particle characteristics.

sections.title: Photon Momentum
objectives: Relate the linear momentum of a photon to its energy or wavelength, and apply linear momentum conservation to simple processes involving the emission, absorption, or reflection of photons.
Account qualitatively for the increase of photon wavelength that is observed, and explain the significance of the Compton wavelength.

misconceptions.claim: A photon is a particle and never behaves as a wave.
misconceptions.correction: It behaves as a particle when it is absorbed or emitted, and as a wave when it passes through a double slit.

summary: Photons have momentum, given by p=hλ, where λ is the photon wavelength.
Photon energy and momentum are related by p=Ec, where E=hf=hc/λ for a photon.

sections.title: The Particle-Wave Duality
objectives: Explain what the term particle-wave duality means, and why it is applied to EM radiation.
Explain how the double-slit experiment with electrons demonstrates particle-wave duality.
Describe when a quantum object behaves more like a particle and when more like a wave.

misconceptions.claim: An electron is either a particle or a wave, and never both.
misconceptions.correction: An electron shows particle-like behaviour in some experiments and wave-like behaviour in others. The two descriptions are complementary, not exclusive.

misconceptions.claim: Wave-particle duality means a particle physically oscillates as it travels.
misconceptions.correction: Duality means the quantum object is described by a wavefunction whose probability amplitude can interfere. The particle is detected as a whole at one place.

summary: EM radiation can behave like either a particle or a wave.
This is termed particle-wave duality.

authored_exercises.stem: What is meant by wave-particle duality?
authored_exercises.answer: Quantum objects such as electrons and photons show both wave-like and particle-like properties depending on the experiment.
solution: A photon delivers its energy in a localized packet.
Electrons produce interference and diffraction patterns.
Both descriptions are needed for a complete account.

authored_exercises.stem: In the double-slit experiment with electrons, what pattern builds up when many electrons are detected?
authored_exercises.answer: An interference pattern of bright and dark fringes.
solution: Each electron is detected at a single point.
The arrival points are not distributed evenly.
The statistical pattern of many electrons is an interference pattern.

authored_exercises.stem: Why is the particle behaviour of an electron most obvious when it hits a detector?
authored_exercises.answer: The detector records the electron at one localized place, so the interaction looks like a particle event.
solution: The electron’s wavefunction spreads through the apparatus.
The detector interaction is localized in space and time.
Detection therefore yields a particle-like spot, while many spots form a wave-like pattern.

sections.title: The Wave Nature of Matter
objectives: Describe the Davisson-Germer experiment, and explain how it provides evidence for the wave nature of electrons.
Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of a particle from its momentum.

misconceptions.claim: Only electrons have a de Broglie wavelength.
misconceptions.correction: Every moving particle has a de Broglie wavelength, λ = h/p. The wavelength is noticeable only when the momentum is very small.

summary: Particles of matter also have a wavelength, called the de Broglie wavelength, given by λ=hp, where p is momentum.
Matter is found to have the same interference characteristics as any other wave.

sections.title: Probability: The Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
objectives: Use both versions of Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle in calculations.
Explain the implications of Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle for measurements.

misconceptions.claim: The uncertainty principle is caused by imperfect measuring instruments.
misconceptions.correction: It is a fundamental property of quantum states, not a technical limitation. A state with a sharply defined position necessarily has a broad spread of momentum.

summary: Matter is found to have the same interference characteristics as any other wave.
There is now a probability distribution for the location of a particle rather than a definite position.

Another consequence of the wave character of all particles is the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which limits the precision with which certain physical quantities can be known simultaneously. For position and momentum, the uncertainty principle is ΔxΔp≥h4π, where Δx is the uncertainty in position and Δp is the uncertainty in momentum.

sections.title: The Particle-Wave Duality Reviewed
objectives: Explain the concept of particle-wave duality, and its scope.
Explain why classical physics emerges from quantum physics for large objects.

misconceptions.claim: Quantum physics replaces classical physics completely, so classical physics is simply wrong.
misconceptions.correction: Quantum physics is the deeper theory, but classical physics emerges as an excellent approximation for large objects and high quantum numbers. Both descriptions are useful in their domains.

summary: The particle-wave duality refers to the fact that all particles-those with mass and those without mass-have wave characteristics.
This is a further connection between mass and energy.
